title: moe-routing-long-context-benchmarks
content:
Purpose:
This doc captures experiment notes and profiling observations from targeted benchmarks comparing dense and MoE variants across Llama, Mistral, and Qwen families, with an emphasis on long-context scaling (8k, 32k, 64k tokens) and MoE routing overhead under production serving conditions. Goal: actionable mitigations for the runtime (kernel selection, batching heuristics, routing optimizations) and a short recommended next-step plan.

Summary of main findings (TL;DR):
- MoE models show attractive FLOP efficiency but exhibit 20–70% throughput variability due to routing hotspotting and memory fragmentation on single-GPU serving.
- Long-context dense models (32k+) are dominated by KV-cache memory bandwidth and attention kernel scaling; throughput drops non-linearly beyond ~16k in our current Triton-backed attention implementation.
- Qwen-like architectures (wider FF layers, shallower attn heads) trade latency for lower per-token memory pressure; in some configs they beat Llama at 8k but lose at 64k due to kv-layout inefficiencies.
- Fast wins: reduce padding and prefer per-request prefix caching; Medium-term wins: routing-load-aware batching and locality-aware expert placement; Long-term: fusion of routing + expert kernels to reduce kernel launch overhead.

Testbed and methodology:
- Hardware: A100 80GB (persistence mode), 2x A100 for multi-GPU runs, occasional H100 spot checks.
- Runtime build: serving-runtime @ commit c3f7b4 (custom Triton kernels enabled), CUDA 12.2, cuBLASLt for matmuls, PyTorch 2.2.0 for model loading.
- Profilers used: nsight-system (aggregated traces), torch.profiler (CPU/CUDA op times), nvtx markers in runtime, and occasional nvprof runs for kernel-level stats.
- Load generator: synthetic streaming traffic via our streaming client (p50 interarrival), mixes: chat-like (prompt 1–3k tokens + 512 gen) and doc-completion (8k–64k prompt + short gen).
- Metrics captured: tokens/sec (steady-state), p50/p95/p99 generation latency, GPU mem peak, number of kernel launches per token, expert dispatch imbalance (stddev of tokens/expert), and device-side host-to-device memcpy time per request.

Experiment matrix (short):
- Models: Llama-2-like 13B dense, hypothetical Llama-MoE-30B (8 experts), Mistral-in-13B-dense, Mistral-MoE-Variant-20B (16 experts), Qwen-14B-dense.
- Contexts: 2k, 8k, 32k, 64k.
- Batch sizes: 1, 4, 16 (where memory permits).
- Quantization: fp16 baseline; 4-bit QAT-lite on a subset.

Key profiling observations by topic:
1) Kernel launch overhead and tiny-kernel fragmentation
- For MoE inference, each token generates: gating kernel (dispatch indices), scatter/gather to experts (small GEMMs), expert local FFN kernels, and a gather. On our build this leads to 6–12 separate CUDA kernel launches per active expert per token.
- When many experts are lightly loaded, the number of launches explodes and per-launch latency dominates, especially at batch size 1. For 8-expert model at bs=1, kernel-launch latency accounted for ~35% of token latency (nsight timelines show many <50us kernels).
- Recommendation: prioritize merging small expert kernels into a fused dispatch+FFN kernel (engineering spike: Triton fused expert kernels).

2) Routing imbalance and hot experts
- Gating softmax tends to select a small subset of experts for short prompts and skewed inputs (we recorded top-2 experts getting ~60% of tokens on average for the Mistral-MoE variant).
- Hotspotting increases memory contention (multiple streams touching same expert memory) and causes stalls due to serialization at mutexes in our current expert queue.
- Short-term mitigation: apply a random jitter to gating logits at serving time (small temperature anneal) which redistributed load and improved tokens/sec by ~8% in a microbench.

3) KV cache memory bandwidth and layout for long-context
- Dense long-context cases are constrained by KV cache reads/writes; our current layout is per-layer contiguous with stride-by-batch, which is suboptimal for long sequences since it leads to scattered accesses during attention.
- At 32k tokens, KV read latency and PCIe/NVLink transfers (for multi-GPU sharded KV) accounted for >40% of p95 latency.
- A layout change (interleaved-by-seq-chunk with blocking) reduced memory traffic and improved throughput by ~18% on 32k benchmarks (engineering note: requires reindexing support in runtime and careful alignment).

4) Attention kernel scaling ceiling
- Our Triton attention kernel scales well to ~8k tokens, but beyond that the memory working set exceeds L2 cache assumptions and kernel runtime increases superlinearly.
- For Llama-like models at 64k we observed 2.8x increase in per-token time vs 8k, whereas theoretical FLOP scaling would suggest ~8x — so memory system is the bottleneck, not compute.
- Consider implementing blocked attention streaming (chunked attention + local context) for very long contexts when exact global attention is not required.

5) Quantization interactions
- 4-bit QAT reduces memory pressure, but MoE expert kernels suffer from lower arithmetic intensity on int4 GEMMs and experience lower throughput than expected because our int4 kernels are not yet well-optimized for small expert sizes.
- For dense long contexts, int4 helped: memory-bound attention kernels saw ~30% mem bandwidth reduction and ~20% throughput gain. For MoE, net effect was model and expert-size dependent.

Representative numbers (A100 80GB, p50 steady-state, bs=1 unless noted):
- Llama-13B dense, 8k prompt: 550 tokens/sec, p95 120ms, GPU mem 34GB.
- Llama-13B dense, 32k prompt: 210 tokens/sec, p95 430ms, GPU mem 46GB.
- Mistral-13B dense, 8k: 630 tokens/sec (tighter heads => slightly better throughput), 32k: 260 tokens/sec.
- Llama-MoE-30B (8 experts), 8k: 720 tokens/sec but with 40% variance over runs; hot expert stalls visible.
- Mistral-MoE-20B (16 experts), 8k: 680 tokens/sec, dispatch imbalance stddev 0.48 (tokens/expert normalized), bs=4 reduces variance.
- Qwen-14B dense, 8k: 760 tokens/sec, 32k: 290 tokens/sec; Qwen shows better 8k perf due to FF layout but loses at 64k.

Operational impacts and notes:
- Serving SLOs: for bs=1 low-latency endpoints, MoE introduces jitter that may violate strict p95 targets unless we implement routing-tail mitigation.
- Cost vs throughput: MoE models can reduce inference cost at similar average throughput but increase tail latency and operational complexity. For synchronous APIs, this is a tradeoff — for async/batched workloads MoE is more attractive.
- Monitoring: need to surface expert-load metrics in Console (per-expert token counts, stddev, recent gating entropy) and an alert when any expert > 3x mean load for >30s.

Immediate recommendations (next 6 weeks):
- Engineering spike to prototype fused expert kernels in Triton (estimated 2–3 engineer-weeks).
- Change KV layout to blocked/interleaved as an opt-in config for long-context routes; run regression tests across 8k/32k/64k.
- Add small-gating-jitter as a configurable runtime flag to spread expert load when tail latency alarms fire.
- Add per-expert telemetry and a dashboard in Console; include gating entropy and expert imbalance charts.

Medium-term (quarter roadmap):
- Routing-aware batching: group requests that route to similar expert sets to reduce memory churn and improve cache locality.
- Explore hybrid attention: local-window + periodic global for ultra-long contexts to reduce KV working set.
- Optimize int4 kernels for small-expert FFNs or fallback logic to fp16 for small experts.

Open questions (for follow-up experiments):
- How does H100 change the kernel-launch vs compute balance for MoE at bs=1 (we only ran a handful of H100 checks)?
- Can model-side gating regularization (during fine-tuning) reduce runtime hotspotting without hurting quality?
- Is there a practical consistent hashing placement for experts across multi-GPU that minimizes cross-device memcpy?

Action items (owners):
- Aisha: prototype gating jitter flag + run 2wk stability test (due 2026-03-20).
- Evan: spike fused Triton expert kernel (pair with Marina) (due 2026-04-10).
- Marina: implement KV blocked layout prototype and perf regression suite for 32k/64k (due 2026-04-01).

Appendix: links to traces and raw data
- nsight traces for sample runs (A100): https://s3.internal.redwood/perf/nsight/moe-8exp-8k-2025-11-18.trace
- raw CSVs and scripts: https://github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/tree/main/benchmarks/long-context

Notes-to-self / loose ideas:
- Consider experiment with elastic expert throttling: cap tokens/expert per-second and fallback to next expert to bound tail.
- Evaluate whether a tiny local expert cache (per-stream) speeds up repeated small-chat workloads.
- Keep an eye on vendor kernels for int4 small-matmul improvements.

End of doc.
